title: Setting up a bantam coop
subtitle: Sizing, perch height, nesting, and ventilation for small-breed chickens.
excerpt: Bantams are roughly a quarter to a third the size of standard breeds, and a bantam coop reflects that difference. The birds need less floor area, lower perches, and smaller pop-holes, but the key principles of good ventilation, draught-free roosting, and secure predator protection are identical. This guide covers the specifics that trip up keepers who downsize from full-size birds.
sourceNotes: Victoria Roberts, Keeping Bantams (Crowood Press, 2011). Chris Graham, Haynes Chicken Manual (2nd edn., 2012). Gail Damerow, Storey's Guide to Raising Chickens (4th edn., 2017), housing chapter.

glossaryTerms.definition: The small door in a chicken coop through which birds enter and exit the coop into the run.
The linear length of roosting perch available per bird. Adequate perch space prevents competition and bullying at roosting time.

content.text: A bantam coop can be smaller than a full-size coop, but the per-bird space allowances remain proportional. Bantams roosting too tightly together develop feather-pecking problems. Get the fundamentals right for the number of birds you are keeping before worrying about aesthetics.

Allow 0.09 to 0.1 m2 of floor area per bantam (versus 0.2 to 0.25 m2 for a large fowl). For 6 bantams, a coop floor of 0.6 m x 1 m is adequate, assuming they free-range or have a run. Internal headroom of 50 to 60 cm is plenty; bantams do not need the standing room a large bird requires.

Bantam perches should be 30 to 40 cm from the floor. Full-size coop perches at 60 to 90 cm are too high for many bantam breeds; they jump, miss, and can injure their legs. The perch should be 3 to 4 cm in diameter: wide enough that the foot can curl round it without the claws touching the front face. Allow 15 to 20 cm of
: 20 cm x 20 cm is adequate for most bantam breeds. Standard large-fowl pop-holes (30 x 30 cm) are not too large, just allow more draught and predator access.
Nest boxes: 25 cm x 25 cm x 25 cm per box. Allow one nest box for every 4 bantam hens; they often lay in the same box regardless, but competition is reduced with more than one.

Ventilation prevents ammonia from rising to damaging concentrations from droppings. In a bantam coop, which has lower internal volume, the ammonia concentration can rise faster than in a larger coop for the same number of birds. Fit ventilation openings on the upper walls or eaves, protected with hardware cloth and a rain baffle, so air can circulate without a direct draught hitting the perch.

Bantams are lighter than large fowl and more vulnerable to aerial predators as well as ground-based ones. If you free-range bantams, overhead netting or frequent supervision is worth the effort. A small bird can pass through gaps that would stop a large chicken; check the coop and run for gaps at 3 cm or less before adding birds.

attrs.cue: Bantams refusing to use the perch and roosting on the floor
attrs.cause: Perch too high, wrong diameter, or heavily contaminated with red mite
attrs.fix: Lower the perch or add a lower step perch as a launch pad. Check for red mite (tiny red or grey specks in crevices, especially where the perch meets the wall). Treat with licenced acaricide and clean the perch with boiling water.

attrs.cue: Hens laying outside the nest box on the floor
attrs.cause: Nest box too small, positioned too high, too dark, or occupied by a broody hen
attrs.fix: Ensure the nest box is at a comfortable stepping-in height and filled with dry straw. If a broody is occupying the box, move her at night to a separate area.
